concepts.name: INC's Early Reluctance to Embrace Peasant Causes (Pre-1920s)
key_dimensions: Moderate-dominated INC's focus on elite constitutional demands vs. agrarian grievances
Why INC avoided direct confrontation with zamindars and landlords who were also Congress supporters
Contrast with later Gandhian phase: what changed and what remained the same
UPSC trap: conflating INC's sympathy for peasants with active organizational support — they were not the same before 1920

concepts.name: Gandhi's Champaran Satyagraha (1917) as a Turning Point in INC-Peasant Interface
key_dimensions: Specific grievances: tinkathia system, indigo cultivation, and rack-renting by European planters
Gandhi's method: fact-finding inquiry vs. direct confrontation — significance of this approach
Outcome: Champaran Agrarian Act 1918 — what it did and did NOT address (limited relief, no land redistribution)
UPSC trap: Champaran is often seen as full peasant integration into INC — but Gandhi explicitly avoided challenging the zamindari system itself

concepts.name: Kheda Satyagraha (1918): INC Support for Peasants Against Colonial Revenue Demands
key_dimensions: Context: crop failure and the demand for revenue suspension under existing rules
Gandhi's 'constructive' approach: using existing legal provisions rather than systemic challenge
Partial success and its ambiguity: government quietly conceded but made no formal announcement
Distinction from Champaran: Kheda targeted colonial state, not Indian landlords — revealing INC's selective peasant advocacy

concepts.name: Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) and Peasant Mobilization: Opportunities and Limits
key_dimensions: How NCM created a pan-India platform that drew peasant participation (e.g., Awadh Kisan Sabha merging with NCM)
Gandhi's discomfort with peasant violence: Chauri Chaura (1922) and withdrawal of the movement
INC's dilemma: peasants radicalized the movement beyond INC's comfort zone
UPSC trap: Chauri Chaura withdrawal — framed as moral choice but also reflects INC's class character and fear of social revolution

concepts.name: Eka Movement (1921–22) and INC's Ambiguous Role
key_dimensions: Origins in Hardoi, Bahraich, Sitapur — led by Madari Pasi, a lower-caste leader outside INC mainstream
Demands: fair rents, against forced labour (begar), against illegal evictions
INC's limited engagement: Eka remained largely outside formal INC structure despite temporal overlap with NCM
UPSC angle: illustrates how INC's peasant mobilization was often channeled through upper-caste intermediaries, marginalizing radical agrarian voices

concepts.name: Awadh Kisan Movement (1920–21) and the Baba Ramchandra Episode
key_dimensions: Baba Ramchandra's independent peasant mobilization vs. Nehru's attempt to bring it under INC umbrella
Formation of Oudh Kisan Sabha and its relationship with Congress — cooperation but not absorption
Peasant demands (nazar abolition, rent reduction) that went beyond what INC officially endorsed
UPSC trap: Nehru's involvement creates illusion of full INC support — but INC leadership consistently moderated radical demands

concepts.name: All India Kisan Sabha (AIKS) Formation (1936) and INC's Tactical Alliance
key_dimensions: Founded at Lucknow alongside INC session — deliberate spatial and temporal proximity signaling alliance
Key figures: Swami Sahajanand Saraswati (president), N.G. Ranga — ideological differences within AIKS leadership
INC's support: tactical (to broaden mass base for 1937 elections) vs. ideological commitment to agrarian reform
UPSC trap: AIKS was affiliated with but NOT part of INC — it was an autonomous body, and this distinction matters

concepts.name: INC's Agrarian Programme and the 1936 Faizpur Session
key_dimensions: First INC session held in a village — symbolic significance of Faizpur choice
Agrarian resolutions passed: debt relief, security of tenure, reduction of rent — compare with actual implementation post-1937
Role of Nehru in drafting agrarian programme: socialist rhetoric vs. Gandhian landlord-friendly practice
UPSC angle: gap between Faizpur promises and Congress provincial government actions (1937–39) as evidence of INC's class limitations

concepts.name: Congress Provincial Governments (1937–39) and Agrarian Reform: Promise vs. Performance
key_dimensions: Which provinces had Congress governments: UP, Bihar, Madras, CP, Orissa, Bombay — and varying agrarian policies
Rent reduction and debt relief measures: Tenancy Acts passed but zamindari abolition deliberately avoided
Growing rift between AIKS (demanding abolition of zamindari) and Congress ministries (protecting landlord interests)
UPSC trap: Congress governments are often praised for peasant welfare — but AIKS publicly criticized them for inadequate reform

concepts.name: Swami Sahajanand Saraswati's Critique of INC and the Break with Congress
key_dimensions: Initial collaboration with INC vs. growing disillusionment post-1937 Congress provincial governance
His argument: INC represented landlord and capitalist interests, not genuine peasant interests
Formation of All India Kisan Sabha's leftward shift and proximity to Communist Party of India
UPSC angle: Sahajanand's trajectory illustrates the structural limits of INC's peasant alliance — radical agrarianism had no permanent home in INC

concepts.name: N.G. Ranga and the 'Kisan-Congress' Moderate Line within AIKS
key_dimensions: Ranga's ideology: peasants as a class distinct from workers — agrarian liberalism vs. Sahajanand's radicalism
Ranga's consistent support for INC vs. Sahajanand's break — illustrating the internal divide in peasant movement
Ranga's later role in founding Swatantra Party — retrospective evidence of his ideological trajectory
UPSC trap: AIKS is often treated as monolithic — the Ranga vs. Sahajanand fault line reveals its ideological plurality

concepts.name: Quit India Movement (1942) and Spontaneous Peasant Participation
key_dimensions: Peasant violence in Bihar, UP, Midnapore — destruction of colonial infrastructure (railways, telegraph)
INC's top leadership was arrested immediately — movement became leaderless and therefore more radical at grassroots
Satara 'Prati Sarkar' (parallel government) in Maharashtra: peasant self-governance beyond INC control
UPSC angle: QIM shows peasants acting IN the name of INC but BEYOND INC's intended framework — revealing autonomous peasant agency

concepts.name: Tebhaga Movement (1946–47) and INC's Response
key_dimensions: Demand for two-thirds share of crop for sharecroppers in Bengal — led by Kisan Sabha under CPI influence
INC Bengal government's response: initially conciliatory but ultimately used police repression
Conflict between INC's electoral calculations (landlord votes) and peasant demands
UPSC trap: Tebhaga is often grouped with 'INC-led' peasant movements — it was explicitly a LEFT-led movement that Congress suppressed

concepts.name: Telangana Movement (1946–51) and INC's Counterinsurgency Role
key_dimensions: Nizam's Hyderabad, Andhra Mahasabha, and Communist-led armed peasant uprising against feudal oppression
INC's military action (police action 1948) against Hyderabad — framed as national integration but also ended peasant gains
Land redistributed during the movement (1 million acres) reversed after INC-led government crackdown
UPSC angle: clearest example of INC actively opposing a peasant movement — tests understanding that INC was not uniformly pro-peasant

concepts.name: Gandhi's Constructive Programme and Its Implications for Peasant Mobilization
key_dimensions: Village uplift, khadi, sanitation — addressed rural poverty without challenging agrarian class structure
Why Gandhi opposed class struggle: concept of trusteeship and landlord-peasant harmony
Contrast with socialist Congressmen (Nehru, Bose) who wanted structural agrarian reform
UPSC trap: Gandhi's pro-peasant image vs. his deliberate avoidance of anti-zamindar mobilization — crucial distinction

concepts.name: Congress Socialist Party (CSP) and Its Role as Bridge Between INC and Agrarian Radicalism
key_dimensions: Founded 1934 by Jayaprakash Narayan, Acharya Narendra Dev, Minoo Masani — within INC but pushing for socialist agenda
CSP's role in organizing AIKS and radicalized peasant wings within Congress fold
Tension with Gandhi and right-wing Congress: CSP's eventual marginalization within INC
UPSC angle: CSP represents the 'what could have been' — a genuinely pro-peasant INC tendency that was ultimately subordinated

concepts.name: INC's Zamindari Abolition Promise and Post-Independence Implementation
key_dimensions: 1929 Lahore session and subsequent resolutions promising land reform — decades-long gap before action
Post-independence zamindari abolition acts (1950s) — implemented by Congress governments but with generous compensation to zamindars
Ceiling legislation and its loopholes: 'voluntary transfers' to family members to evade ceilings
UPSC trap: INC did abolish zamindari — but the manner of abolition (with compensation, with loopholes) reflects its class character

concepts.name: The 'Class Character' Debate: Was INC a Bourgeois-Landlord Party or a Multi-Class Coalition?
key_dimensions: Marxist historiography (R.P. Dutt, A.R. Desai): INC as representative of capitalist and landlord interests
Nationalist historiography: INC as genuinely broad-based national movement with peasant participation
Evidence for both sides: Champaran (pro-peasant) vs. Telangana suppression (anti-peasant)
UPSC angle: this debate directly shapes how to answer questions about INC-peasant relationship — both 'INC championed peasants' and 'INC limited peasant movements' can be argued with evidence

concepts.name: Role of Local Congress Leaders vs. Central INC Leadership in Peasant Movements
key_dimensions: Local leaders (e.g., Baba Ramchandra in Awadh, Vallabhbhai Patel in Bardoli) often more willing to support peasants than central INC
Central INC leadership's moderation of local Congress-peasant alliances to protect national political consensus
Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) as example: Patel's success with limited demand (revenue suspension) vs. avoiding tenancy reform
UPSC trap: success of Bardoli is often cited as INC-peasant unity — but Bardoli was specifically a prosperous peasant movement, not a movement of the rural poor

concepts.name: Comparative Framework: INC's Differential Engagement with Peasant vs. Tribal Movements
key_dimensions: INC more willing to support peasant movements (economically legible demands) than tribal movements (territorial/cultural autonomy demands)
Tribal movements (Rampa, Santhal, Tana Bhagat) largely remained outside INC's organizational embrace
Scheduled Areas provisions in Constitution vs. INC's developmental agenda — continuity of marginalization
UPSC angle: this comparison reveals that INC's peasant engagement, however limited, was still significantly greater than its tribal engagement
